title: Hyperlane Cloudworks - Onramp & integration friction points
summary: Introductory partner discovery to evaluate Hyperlane as a channel/reseller for Redwood Dedicated and Private onramp. Key themes: VPC and peering constraints, GPU SKUs and scheduling, latency vs cost tradeoffs, integration touchpoints (KMS, SSO), pilot framing and benchmarks. Agreed next steps include sharing integration checklist, scheduling architecture deep dive, and providing test access for basic throughput runs.
topics: Latency vs cost and batching strategies
action_items: Maya Patel|Share Redwood partner onramp deck and integration checklist|2026-04-12
Connor Li|Schedule architecture deep dive and bring infra diagrams|2026-04-16
Jules Martinez|Provide Hyperlane test VPC details and contact for network team|2026-04-14
Priya Kapoor|Confirm commercial model interest (reseller vs referral)|2026-04-20
next_steps: Redwood to send partner integration checklist + shared deck (Maya)
Schedule 1.5h architecture deep dive with Hyperlane infra and network (Connor)

transcript:
Meeting header:
Date: 2026-04-09 14:00 PDT
Duration: 46 minutes
Recording: yes
Attendees: Maya (Redwood AE), Connor (Redwood SE), Jules M (Hyperlane Head of Integrations), Priya K (Cloud Partnerships), Evan R (SRE Lead)

[00:00] Maya: Hey everyone, thanks for joining, um, this is Maya from Redwood Inference. I think we have Connor from our infra team, and from Hyperlane we have Jules, Priya, and Evan, thanks for making time. Quick agenda is partner onramp discovery, how Hyperlane thinks about reselling or integrating Redwood Dedicated/Private, and surface any infra or security blockers. Does that sound right?
[00:16] Jules: Yeah that sounds good. Quick thing: we're exploring multiple onramps and want to see if Redwood fits our reseller model and also technical on-prem customers.
[00:28] Connor: Awesome, I can talk low-level infra, kernel selection, batching, quantization tradeoffs, that sort of thing. And we can talk about routing/fallbacks across host vs dedicated.
[00:39] Priya: Also commercial question — do you support both referral and white-label reseller contracts? Not a legal deep dive, just top-level.
[00:47] Maya: High level yes, we have both referral and reserved capacity models, and for enterprise we do partner agreements. We'll follow up with formal terms, but for the POC we usually do a consumption pilot or a small dedicated commit.
[00:58] Evan: From SRE side I'm most worried about network isolation and key mgmt — we have strict KMS rules and we can't allow model keys to be exported. Also VPC peering is a must for some customers.
[01:12] Connor: Totally — our Private deployment supports customer-managed KMS/HSM and VPC peering and on-prem variants. In some notes, the KMS integration can be via customer KMS endpoints or through managed indicates — sorry, managed KMS proxies, which I know can sound fuzzy in a transcript.
[01:30] Jules: Right, specifically: we need to know if peering will allow cross-AZ traffic and whether Redwood's agent needs inbound ports opened. Also, can you run inside our subnet without NAT?
[01:44] Connor: Yes, Private can be deployed as a customer-controlled control plane with no egress to public internet if desired. There are two modes — one is VPC peering where our control plane talks to a connector, the other is fully air-gapped on-prem with an offline bundle. Both require some iptables and port config; we'll share the infra diagram.
[02:02] Priya: When you say connector, is that a lightweight agent or a heavy gateway? Our security ops will want to know process ownership and patching cadence.
[02:12] Connor: It's a small bridge process, stateless mostly, runs in the customer's VPC. Patch cadence is aligned to our private release train, but security patches are pushed as hotfixes when needed. We can also hand over the image for Hyperlane to bake.
[02:27] Maya: From GTM — once we establish the technical feasibility, we can talk through margins and packaging. But for devs, they're going to ask about latency, token cost, and throughput.
[02:39] Jules: On latency — some of our customers are very latency-sensitive for chat product features. What's real-world tail latency for short-turn prompts on Dedicated?
[02:50] Connor: For a 2k token LRU and typical gpt-variant we see p50 around 80–120ms on A100-like SKUs with optimized kernels, p95 can vary based on batching patterns. The trick is that batching reduces cost but increases tail. We have continuous batching and prefix caching to reduce that impact.
[03:09] Evan: Are you using NCCL multi-GPU for KV cache sharing or sharded inference? We have customers who want to avoid cross-host KV syncing because it complicates autoscaling.
[03:19] Connor: We try to avoid cross-host KV sync for inference; most of our sharding is at model partitioning or via multiple model replicas. For KV cache we keep it local and use sticky routing when low latency matters. There are cases where we use NCCL for multi-GPU within a node, but cross-node NCCL is more for training.
[03:34] Jules: Good to know. Can you support mixed SKUs? For saleable product we want to offer a cheap burst (T4) and a premium low-latency (A100/H100) SKU.
[03:46] Maya: Yes — routing policies can be configured to tier by latency/SLO and cost. Redwood's smart routing will fallback to compatible model variants. You can present two SKUs in your catalog.
[03:56] [04:00] Priya: Ok, on the security side, SOC2 and ISO are standard asks — do you publish those reports and do you allow us to circulate the AOC to customers?
[04:10] Maya: We have SOC2 Type II and ISO 27001; we'll share the atlas and the AOC with an NDA. For Private deployments, many controls are customer-managed so the scope narrows.
[04:22] Evan: Also curious about audit logs and RBAC granularity — do you support token-level tracing? We need per-tenant logging for compliance.
[04:31] Connor: Our console supports token-level cost and latency breakdowns, and we emit audit logs to customer-owned logging endpoints. RBAC supports role scoping down to model and route levels. There are some naming slight variances in our console vs official doc — sometimes the UI calls it 'routes' where the API uses 'endpoints' — apologies for the mismatch.
[04:55] Maya: No worries. Let's talk pilot. Jules, what would success look like for Hyperlane? What's the minimum to show to channel partners?
[05:05] Jules: For go/no-go we need: 1) a network-validated deployment in our test VPC, 2) a short benchmark showing 2x of our current throughput for cost parity, 3) security docs and a simple reseller T&C draft. If those check out, we can list Redwood as a preferred integration.
[05:23] Maya: Good checklist. For the benchmark, Connor, what do we need to run?
[05:28] Connor: We usually ask for a small test VPC with a couple of instances and some sample prompt sets. We'll run a throughput sweep with varying sequence lengths and batching configs. Also we'll need sample traffic distribution and success metrics — do you have a canonical prompt set?
[05:41] Jules: We can provide a redacted prompt set and distribution — typical chat messages are 20–60 tokens, embeddings workload is separate. We'll send that over.
[05:49] Evan: Network wise, we will open peering but need to know IP ranges and ports. What's the default port and do you require inbound?
[05:57] Connor: The connector uses outbound to our control plane by default, and for some Private modes you can have the control plane inside your VPC. We'll send a network matrix with ports; commonly 443 and a small range for health checks. I will double-check the exact ephemeral ports.
[06:12] Priya: Commercially, how are margins split for reseller? Ballpark numbers are fine now.
[06:18] Maya: We have a reseller program with tiered margins based on committed capacity and co-sell involvement. I'll loop legal/partner ops after this call; right now it's best to frame a pilot and then discuss margins once usage contours are known.
[06:29] Jules: Fine. Another technical Q — does Redwood support quantized model variants out of the box? Some of our customers want int8 or 4-bit models to reduce cost.
[06:39] Connor: Yes, we support quantized variants and maintain model catalog entries for q4/q8 where available. We also provide recommended quantization profiles per workload in Redwood Optimize. Note that quality regressions are tracked via our eval hooks.
[06:52] Jules: Good. Any gotchas with quantized models and private deployments?
[06:56] Connor: The main ones are kernel availability and hardware compatibility. Some kernels for q4 are optimized for specific GPU architectures; we recommend testing the exact SKU. We'll include recommended GPU/driver pairs in the integration doc.
[07:12] Maya: Ok, I'm going to capture the action items, but before that, any blockers from Hyperlane's side?
[07:20] Evan: Two quick things: 1) we need a clear SLA for Dedicated commitments for our customers, and 2) we need clarity on support model — is Redwood support 24/7 for reseller escalations?
[07:32] Maya: For Dedicated we offer SLA-backed uptimes and can align on escalation paths; premium support is available. We'll include an escalation matrix in the partner packet.
[07:41] Priya: Also, any experience integrating with marketplace billing systems? We have a custom billing connector.
[07:48] Maya: We have done marketplace integrations before; sometimes it's through a metering API or invoice pass-through. We'll surface examples.
[07:56] [08:00] Connor: One more infra note — for large multi-tenant customers we recommend keeping model replicas per-tenant for privacy or using Private. The routing layer can handle tenant pinning, but you need capacity isolation for noisy neighbors.
[08:14] Jules: That dovetails with our customers who demand tenancy guarantees. We need to map out deployment patterns: shared-hosted, dedicated per-tenant, and fully private.
[08:25] Maya: We'll prepare a decision matrix. Connor, should we propose a recommended pattern for 3 customer archetypes?
[08:31] Connor: Yes — archetype A (PLG chat app) = hosted with prefix caching; B (regulated enterprise) = Private with VPC peering and KMS; C (high throughput batch) = Dedicated reserved GPU pool with autoscale. We'll send details.
[08:47] Jules: Nice. On legal — procurement will want vendor questionnaires. Can you fill out a standard security questionnaire?
[08:53] Maya: Yes, we can. We'll return the vendor questionnaire, and if needed we'll set a security review call with our security lead.
[09:02] Evan: For the benchmark, can you simulate our ingress patterns? We have lots of short messages with occasional long context. The tail behavior is important.
[09:11] Connor: Absolutely. We'll need sample traces; if you can send a 24-48 hour sample (anonymized) that'll help shape batching configs.
[09:21] Priya: A minor ask — can we white-label the console for channel partners? Our partners want a co-branded onboarding feel.
[09:30] Maya: There's some flexibility on branding for partner portals; we can discuss product-marketing involvement. For the POC, we'll prioritize functionality over branding.
[09:39] Jules: Understood. Anything else?
[09:43] Maya: I'll go through a rapid recap and owners. Connor — you'll own infra deep dive and benchmark plan. I'll send partner packet and reseller model. Jules/Priya — you'll provision a test VPC and send prompt traces. Evan — you'll coordinate network folks for peering.
[09:58] Jules: Yep we'll do that.
[10:02] Connor: I'll also attach a sample infra diagram and a list of recommended GPU/driver combos for quantized kernels.
[10:10] Maya: Great. We'll follow up with a calendar invite for the 90-minute architecture session. Any last minute notes?
[10:18] Evan: Could you also include a short runbook for incident response? Our SOC wants playbooks.
[10:23] Maya: Yes — we'll include runbook snippets and the escalation matrix.
[10:27] Priya: Thank you all. Looking forward to the deck.
[10:31] Maya: Thanks everyone, we'll follow up.
